newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH FINMIN COMMENT BOOSTS ZLOTY VS BASKET.
newsitem.headline: POLISH FINMIN COMMENT BOOSTS ZLOTY VS BASKET.

text.p: The Polish zloty on Wednesday started to rebound after falling more than two percent over the last four trading days on large-scale foreign investor pullout sparked by the Czech crown's steep decline, dealers said.

Earlier on Wednesday Polish Finance Minister Marek Belka said the main wave of foreign investor withdrawal from zloty instruments has ended, which the market took as a signal to increase the value of the zloty.
"Belka signalled that there was no fundemental reason for keeping the zloty weak and a (currency) selling spree ensued," said Piotr Czyzewski, forex dealer at ING bank in Warsaw.
"More gains could be in store for the zloty," he added.
At 1200 GMT the zloty rebounded to 1.19/1.04 percent stronger than the parity rate, up from 0.47/0.32 percent at opening and Tuesday's intraday lows dipping to parity.
It was at 3.2040/00 to the dollar and at 1.8875/95 to the mark, against opening's 3.2285/50 and 1.8990/20.

Last Thursday and Friday the zloty dropped two percent against the basket of currencies as foreign investors sold the Polish unit to cut their central European exposure after the sharp fall of the Czech crown.
Belka estimated that a total of $1.2 billion of short-term speculative capital was in Poland, which he said was not enough to significantly weaken the zloty even if all of it pulled out.
"I estimate that even if all the short-term, speculative capital left Poland, it would only have a minor effect on the zloty exchange rate," Belka told a news conference.
But he said he did not know how much foreign short-term capital flowed out of Poland during the pullout but quoted press reports which said the sales totalled some $400 million.

He also said the National Bank of Poland's small currency selling intervention last week to stop the zloty's fall proved very effective and made him confident the cental bank was in control of the situation.
Last Friday the NBP bought an estimated $15 million which stopped the zloty in its tracks at just above the parity rate.
Analysts said that Poland's economy, which was now much stronger than the Czech Republic's, would likely keep the zloty from plunging in line with the crown.
